hook_text: Every spring, farmers in the Western Cape rent thousands of beehives. Without them, almost no apples.
clip_script: An apple tree cannot move its pollen. Pollen has to get from the anther to the sticky stigma of another tree, and many apples refuse their own pollen. So farmers truck beehives into the orchards. A bee pushes into a flower for nectar, sticky pollen rubs onto its hairy body, and at the next tree some rubs off. That is pollination. Plants that use the wind do not bother with pretty petals: grass and mealies dangle their anthers and throw clouds of dusty pollen into the air. Plants that use animals advertise with colour, scent and a sweet drink. Sunbirds love red tubes like aloes. Moths love white flowers at night. The strelitzia even gives birds a perch that dusts their feet. And here is the big one: about a third of the food you eat needs pollinators.
visual_style: Whiteboard trucks unloading hives into an orchard; a bee carrying glowing pollen dots between two flowers; a quick split of a dusty grass flower and a bright aloe with a sunbird.
pacing: Punchy farm hook, fast flower comparisons, a strong food-plate finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and spot the courier for every flower you see.
